entries.7c9eb0590a1ef633248e5c8073a13838f364b5e3: <div sID="gen17794" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Jer.27" sID="Jer.27"/> <div eID="gen17794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17795" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17796" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah the prophet, since he cannot persuade people to submit to God's precept, and so to prevent the destruction of their country by the king of Babylon, is here persuading them to submit to God's providence, by yielding tamely to the king of Babylon, and becoming tributaries to him, which was the wisest course they could now take, and would be a mitigation of the calamity, and prevent the laying of their country waste by fire and sword; the sacrificing of their liberties would be the saving of their lives. I. He gives this counsel, in God's name, to the kings of the neighbouring nations, that they might make the best of bad, assuring them that there was no remedy, but they must serve the king of Babylon; and yet in time there should be relief, for his dominion should last but 70 years, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.1-Jer.27.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He gives this counsel to Zedekiah king of Judah particularly (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12-Jer.27.15">ver. 12-15</reference>) and to the priests and people, assuring them that the king of Babylon should still proceed against them till things were brought to the last extremity, and a patient submission would be the only way to mitigate the calamity and make it easy, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16-Jer.27.22">ver. 16-22</reference>. Thus the prophet, if they would but have hearkened to him, would have directed them in the paths of true policy as well as of true piety.
entries.7e9143894bbdca1a7e32fd06425e61d81e3ae5cd: <div eID="gen17796" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17795" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Nebuchadnezzar's Victories Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 597.)</title> <div sID="gen17797" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah came this word unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to me; Make thee bonds and yokes, and put them upon thy neck, <hi type="super">3</hi> And send them to the king of Edom, and to the king of Moab, and to the king of the Ammonites, and to the king of Tyrus, and to the king of Zidon, by the hand of the messengers which come to Jerusalem unto Zedekiah king of Judah; <hi type="super">4</hi> And command them to say unto their masters, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Thus shall ye say unto your masters; <hi type="super">5</hi> I have made the earth, the man and the beast that <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the ground, by my great power and by my outstretched arm, and have given it unto whom it seemed meet unto me. <hi type="super">6</hi> And now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and the beasts of the field have I given him also to serve him. <hi type="super">7</hi> And all nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the very time of his land come: and then many nations and great kings shall serve themselves of him. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the nation and kingdom which will not serve the same Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, and that will not put their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, that nation will I punish, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with the sword, and with the famine, and with the pestilence, until I have consumed them by his hand. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon: <hi type="super">10</hi> For they prophesy a lie unto you, to remove you far from your land; and that I should drive you out, and ye should perish. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the nations that bring their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him, those will I let remain still in their own land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and they shall till it, and dwell therein. <div eID="gen17797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17798" type="x-p"/> Some difficulty occurs in the date of this prophecy. This word is said to come to Jeremiah <hi type="italic">in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">v. 1</reference>), and yet the messengers, to whom he is to deliver the badges of servitude, are said (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">v. 3</reference>) to come to <hi type="italic">Zedekiah king of Judah,</hi> who reigned not till eleven years after the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign. Some make it an error of the copy, and think that it should be read (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah,</hi> for which some negligent scribe, having his eye on the title of the foregoing chapter, wrote <hi type="italic">Jehoiakim.</hi> And, if one would admit a mistake any where, it should be here, for Zedekiah is mentioned again (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12">v. 12</reference>), and the next prophecy is dated the same year, and said to be in the <hi type="italic">beginning of the reign of Zedekiah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">ch. xxviii. 1</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot solves it thus: In the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign Jeremiah is to make these bonds and yokes, and to put them upon his own neck, in token of Judah's subjection to the king of Babylon, which began at that time; but he is to send them to the neighbouring kings afterwards in the reign of Zedekiah, of whose succession to Jehoiakim, and the ambassadors sent to him, mention is made by way of prediction. <div eID="gen17798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17799" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah is to prepare a sign of the general reduction of all these countries into subjection to the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Make thee bonds and yokes,</hi> yokes with bonds to fasten them, that the beast may not slip his neck out of the yoke. Into these the prophet must put his own neck to make them taken notice of as a prophetic representation; for every one would enquire, What is the meaning of Jeremiah's yokes? We find him with one on, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.10">ch. xxviii. 10</reference>. Hereby he intimated that he advised them to nothing but what he was resolved to do himself; for he was not one of those that <hi type="italic">bind heavy burdens</hi> on others, which they themselves will not <hi type="italic">touch with one of their fingers.</hi> Ministers must thus lay themselves under the weight and obligation of what they preach to others. <div eID="gen17799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17800" type="x-p"/> II. He is to send this, with a sermon annexed to it, to all the neighbouring princes; those are mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">v. 3</reference>) that lay next to the land of Canaan. It should seem, there was a treaty of alliance on foot between the king of Judah and all those other kings. Jerusalem was the place appointed for the treaty. Thither they all sent their plenipotentiaries; and it was agreed that they should bind themselves in a league offensive and defensive, to stand by one another, in opposition to the growing threatening greatness of the king of Babylon, and to reduce his exorbitant power. They had great confidence in their strength thus united, and were ready to call themselves the high allies; but, when the envoys were returning to their respective masters with the ratification of this treaty, Jeremiah gives each of them a yoke to carry to his master, to signify to him that he must either by consent or by compulsion become a servant to the king of Babylon, let him choose which he will. In the sermon upon this sign, 1. God asserts his own indisputable right to dispose of kingdoms as he pleases, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.5">v. 5</reference>. He is the Creator of all things; he <hi type="italic">made the earth</hi> at first, established it, and it abides: it is still the same, though <hi type="italic">one generation passes away and another comes.</hi> He still by a continued creation produces <hi type="italic">man and beast upon the ground,</hi> and it is by his <hi type="italic">great power</hi> and <hi type="italic">outstretched arm.</hi> His arm has infinite strength, though it be stretched out. Upon this account he may give and convey a property and dominion to whomsoever he pleases. As he hath graciously <hi type="italic">given the earth to the children of men</hi> in general (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">Ps. cxv. 16</reference>), so he give to each his share of it, be it more or less. Note, Whatever any have of the good things of this world, it is what God sees fit to give them; we ourselves should therefore be content, though we have ever so little, and not envy any their share, though they have ever so much. 2. He publishes a grant of all these countries to Nebuchadnezzar. Know all men by these presents. <hi type="italic">Sciant præsentes et futuri—Let those of the present and those of the future age know.</hi> "This is to certify to all whom it may concern that I have <hi type="italic">given all these lands,</hi> with all the wealth of them, into <hi type="italic">the hands of the king of Babylon;</hi> even the beasts <hi type="italic">of the field,</hi> whether tame or wild, <hi type="italic">have I given to him,</hi> parks and pastures; they are all his own." Nebuchadnezzar was a proud wicked man, an idolater; and yet God, in his providence, gives him this large dominion, these vast possessions. Note, The things of this world are not the best things, for God often gives the largest share of them to bad men, that are rivals with him and rebels against him. He was a wicked man, and yet what he had he had by divine grant. Note, Dominion is not founded in grace. Those that have not any colourable title to eternal happiness may yet have a justifiable title to their temporal good things. Nebuchadnezzar is a very bad man, and yet God calls him his servant, because he employed him as an instrument of his providence for the chastising of the nations, and particularly his own people; and for his service therein he thus liberally repaid him. Those whom God makes use of shall not lose by him; much more will he be found the bountiful rewarder of all those that designedly and sincerely serve him. 3. He assures them that they should all be unavoidably brought under the dominion of the king of Babylon for a time (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">All nations,</hi> all these nations and many others, shall serve <hi type="italic">him, and his son, and his son's son.</hi> His son was Evil-merodach, and his son's son Belshazzar, in whom his kingdom ceased: then the time of reckoning with his land came, when the tables were turned, and <hi type="italic">many nations and great kings,</hi> incorporated into the empire of the Medes and Persians, <hi type="italic">served themselves of him,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">ch. xxv. 14</reference>. Thus Adonibezek was trampled upon himself, as he had trampled on other kings. 4. He threatens those with military execution that stood out and would not submit to the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">v. 8</reference>): That nation that will not <hi type="italic">put their neck under his yoke</hi> I will <hi type="italic">punish with sword and famine,</hi> with one judgment after another, till it is <hi type="italic">consumed by his hand.</hi> Nebuchadnezzar was very unjust and barbarous in invading the rights and liberties of his neighbours thus, and forcing them into a subjection to him; yet God had just and holy ends in permitting him to do so, to punish these nations for their idolatry and gross immoralities. Those that would not serve the God that made them were justly made to serve their enemies that sought to ruin them. 5. He shows them the vanity of all the hopes they fed themselves with, that they should preserve their liberties, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.9-Jer.27.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. These nations had their prophets too, that pretended to foretell future events by the stars, or by dreams, or enchantments; and they, to please their patrons, and because they would themselves have it so, flattered them with assurances that they <hi type="italic">should not serve the king of Babylon.</hi> Thus they designed to animate them to a vigorous resistance; and, though they had no ground for it, they hoped hereby to do them service. But he tells them that it would prove to their destruction; for by resisting they would provoke the conqueror to deal severely with them, to <hi type="italic">remove them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">drive them out</hi> into a miserable captivity, in which they should all be lost and buried in oblivion. Particular prophecies against these nations that bordered on Israel severally, the ruin of which is here foretold in the general, we shall meet with, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.49.39">ch. xlviii. and xlix.</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.1-Ezek.25.17">and Ezek. xxv.</reference>, which had the same accomplishment with this here. Note, <hi type="italic">When God judges he will overcome.</hi> 6. He puts them in a fair way to prevent their destruction by a quiet and easy submission, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.11">v. 11</reference>. The nations that will be content to <hi type="italic">serve the king of Babylon,</hi> and pay him tribute for seventy years (ten apprenticeships), <hi type="italic">those will I let remain still in their own land.</hi> Those that will bend shall not break. Perhaps the dominion of the king of Babylon may bear no harder upon them than that of their own kings had done. It is often more a point of honour than true wisdom to prefer liberty before life. It is not mentioned to the disgrace of Issachar that because he saw <hi type="italic">rest</hi> was <hi type="italic">good,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">land pleasant,</hi> that he might peaceably enjoy it, he bowed <hi type="italic">his shoulder to bear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">became a servant to tribute</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.14-Gen.49.15">Gen. xlix. 14, 15</reference>), as these are here advised to do: <hi type="italic">Serve the king of Babylon and you shall till the land</hi> and <hi type="italic">dwell therein.</hi> Some would condemn this as the evidence of a mean spirit, but the prophet recommends it as that of a meek spirit, which yields to necessity, and by a quiet submission to the hardest turns of Providence makes the best of bad: it is better to do so than by struggling to make it worse. <div eID="gen17800" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen17801"/> <l level="1" sID="gen17802"/>———Levius fit patientia<l eID="gen17802" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen17803"/>Quicquid corrigere est nefas. Hor.<l eID="gen17803" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen17804"/>———When we needs must bear,<l eID="gen17804" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen17805"/>Enduring patience makes the burden light. <hi type="small-caps">Creech</hi> .<l eID="gen17805" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen17801"/> <div sID="gen17806" type="x-p"/> Many might have prevented destroying providences by humbling themselves under humbling providences. It is better to take up a lighter cross in our way than to pull a heavier on our own head.
entries.d21ab584195b949598da8dc370ebeeb4df25518e: <div eID="gen17806" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Counsel to Zedekiah; Submission to Nebuchadnezzar Urged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 597.)</title> <div sID="gen17807" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> I spake also to Zedekiah king of Judah according to all these words, saying, Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live. <hi type="super">13</hi> Why will ye die, thou and thy people, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken against the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore hearken not unto the words of the prophets that speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon: for they prophesy a lie unto you. <hi type="super">15</hi> For I have not sent them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , yet they prophesy a lie in my name; that I might drive you out, and that ye might perish, ye, and the prophets that prophesy unto you. <hi type="super">16</hi> Also I spake to the priests and to all this people, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Hearken not to the words of your prophets that prophesy unto you, saying, Behold, the vessels of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house shall now shortly be brought again from Babylon: for they prophesy a lie unto you. <hi type="super">17</hi> Hearken not unto them; serve the king of Babylon, and live: wherefore should this city be laid waste? <hi type="super">18</hi> But if they <hi type="italic">be</hi> prophets, and if the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be with them, let them now make intercession to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, that the vessels which are left in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem, go not to Babylon. <hi type="super">19</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts concerning the pillars, and concerning the sea, and concerning the bases, and concerning the residue of the vessels that remain in this city, <hi type="super">20</hi> Which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took not, when he carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah from Jerusalem to Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem; <hi type="super">21</hi> Yea, thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that remain <hi type="italic">in</hi> the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the house of the king of Judah and of Jerusalem; <hi type="super">22</hi> They shall be carried to Babylon, and there shall they be until the day that I visit them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; then will I bring them up, and restore them to this place. <div eID="gen17807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17808" type="x-p"/> What was said to all the nations is here with a particular tenderness applied to the nation of the Jews, for whom Jeremiah was sensibly concerned. The case at present stood thus: Judah and Jerusalem had often contested with the king of Babylon, and still were worsted; many both of their valuable persons and their valuable goods were carried to Babylon already, and some of the <hi type="italic">vessels of the Lord's house</hi> particularly. Now how this struggle would issue was the question. They had those among them at Jerusalem who pretended to be prophets, who bade them hold out and they should, in a little time, be too hard for the king of Babylon and recover all that they had lost. Now Jeremiah is sent to bid them yield and knock under, for that, instead of recovering what they had lost, they should otherwise lose all that remained; and to press them to this is the scope of these verses. <div eID="gen17808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17809" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah humbly addresses the king of Judah, to persuade him to surrender to the king of Babylon. His act would be the people's and would determine them, and therefore he speaks to him as to them all (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon and live.</hi> Is it their wisdom to submit to the heavy iron yoke of a cruel tyrant, that they may secure the lives of their bodies? And is it not much more our wisdom to submit to the sweet and easy yoke of our rightful Lord and Master Jesus Christ, that we may secure the lives of our souls? Bring down your spirits to repentance and faith, and that is the way to bring up your spirits to heaven and glory. And with much more cogency and compassion may we expostulate with perishing souls than Jeremiah here expostulates with a perishing people: "<hi type="italic">Why will you die by the sword and the famine</hi>—miserable deaths, which you inevitably run yourselves upon, under pretence of avoiding miserable lives?" What God had spoken, in general, of all those that would not submit to the king of Babylon, he would have them to apply to themselves and be afraid of. It were well if sinners would, in like manner, be afraid of the destruction threatened against all those that will not have <hi type="italic">Christ to reign over them,</hi> and reason thus with themselves, "<hi type="italic">Why should we die</hi> the second death, which is a thousand times worse than that by <hi type="italic">sword and famine,</hi> when we might submit and live?" <div eID="gen17809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17810" type="x-p"/> II. He addresses himself likewise to the priests and the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">v. 16</reference>), to persuade them to <hi type="italic">serve the king of Babylon,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">live,</hi> and might prevent the desolation of the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wherefore should it be laid waste,</hi> as certainly it will be if you stand it out?" The priests had been Jeremiah's enemies, and had sought his life to destroy it, yet he approves himself their friend, and seeks their lives, to preserve and secure them, which is an example to us to render <hi type="italic">good for evil.</hi> When the <hi type="italic">blood-thirsty hate the upright,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">the just seek his soul,</hi> and the welfare of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Prov. xxix. 10</reference>. The matter was far gone here; they were upon the brink of ruin, which they would not have been brought to if they would have taken Jeremiah's counsel; yet he continues his friendly admonitions to them, to save the last stake and manage that wisely, and now at length in this their day to understand the <hi type="italic">things that belong to their peace,</hi> when they had but one day to turn them in. <div eID="gen17810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17811" type="x-p"/> III. In both these addresses he warns them against giving credit to the false prophets that rocked them asleep in their security, because they saw that they loved to slumber: "<hi type="italic">Hearken not to the words of the prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">your prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">v. 16</reference>. They are not God's prophets; he never sent them; they do not serve him, nor seek to please him; they are yours, for they say what you would have them say, and aim at nothing but to please you." Two things their prophets flattered them into the belief of:—1. That the power which the king of Babylon had gained over them should now shortly be broken. They said (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.14">v. 14</reference>), "<hi type="italic">You shall not serve the king of Babylon;</hi> you need not submit voluntarily, for you shall not be compelled to submit." This they prophesied <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.15">v. 15</reference>), as if God had sent them to the people on this errand, in kindness to them, that they might not disparage themselves by an inglorious surrender. But it was a lie. They said that God sent them; but that was false; he disowns it: <hi type="italic">I have not sent them, saith the Lord.</hi> They said that they should never be brought into subjection to the king of Babylon; but that was false too, the event proved it so. They said that to hold out to the last would be the way to secure themselves and their city; but that was false, for it would certainly end in their being driven out and perishing. So that it was all a lie, from first to last; and the prophets that deceived the people with these lies did, in the issue, but deceive themselves; the blind leaders and the blind followers fell together into the ditch: That <hi type="italic">you might perish, you, and the prophets that prophesy unto you,</hi> who will be so far from warranting your security that they cannot secure themselves. Note, Those that encourage sinners to go on in their sinful ways will in the end perish with them. 2. They prophesied that the vessels of the temple, which the king of Babylon had already carried away, should now shortly be brought back (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">v. 16</reference>); this they fed the priests with the hopes of, knowing how acceptable it would be to them, who loved the <hi type="italic">gold of the temple</hi> better than the <hi type="italic">temple that sanctified the gold.</hi> These vessels were taken away when Jeconiah was carried captive into Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">v. 20</reference>. We have the story, and it is a melancholy one, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.13 2Kgs.24.15 2Chr.36.10">2 Kings xxiv. 13, 15; 2 Chron. xxxvi. 10</reference>. All the <hi type="italic">goodly vessels</hi> (that is, all the <hi type="italic">vessels of gold</hi> that were <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord</hi>), with all the treasures, were taken as prey, and brought to Babylon. This was grievous to them above any thing; for the temple was their pride and confidence, and the stripping of that was too plain an indication of that which the true prophet told them, that their <hi type="italic">God had departed from them.</hi> Their false prophets therefore had no other way to make them easy than by telling them that the king of Babylon should be forced to restore them in a little while. Now here, (1.) Jeremiah bids them think of preserving the vessels that remained by their prayers, rather than of bringing back those that were gone by their prophecies (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">If they be prophets,</hi> as they pretend, and if <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord be with them</hi>—if they have any intercourse with heaven and any interest there, let them improve it for the stopping of the progress of the judgment; let them step into the gap, and stand with their censer <hi type="italic">between the living and the dead,</hi> between that which is carried away and that which remains, that <hi type="italic">the plague may be stayed; let them make intercession with the Lord of hosts,</hi> that the vessels which are left go not after the rest. [1.] Instead of prophesying, let them pray. Note, Prophets must be praying men; by being much in prayer they must make it to appear that they keep up a correspondence with heaven. We cannot think that those do, as prophets, ever hear thence, who do not frequently by prayer send thither. By praying for the safety and prosperity of the sanctuary they must make it to appear that, as becomes prophets, they are of a public spirit; and by the success of their prayers it will appear that God favours them. [2.] Instead of being concerned for the retrieving of what they had lost, they must bestir themselves for the securing of what was left, and take it as a great favour if they can gain that point. When God's judgments are abroad we must not seek great things, but be thankful for a little. (2.) He assures them that even this point should not be gained, but the brazen vessels should go after the golden ones, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">v. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.22">22</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar had found so good a booty once that he would be sure to come again and take all he could find, not only in <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord,</hi> but in the <hi type="italic">king's house.</hi> They shall all be carried to Babylon in triumph, and <hi type="italic">there shall they be.</hi> But he concludes with a gracious promise that the time should come when they should all be returned: <hi type="italic">Until the day that I visit them in mercy,</hi> according to appointment, and <hi type="italic">then I will bring</hi> those vessels <hi type="italic">up again, and restore them to this place,</hi> to their place. Surely they were under the protection of a special Providence, else they would have been melted down and put to some other use; but there was to be a second temple, for which they were to be reserved. We read particularly of the return of them, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.8">Ezra i. 8</reference>. Note, Though the return of the church's prosperity do not come in our time, we must not therefore despair of it, for it will come in God's time. Though those who said, <hi type="italic">The vessels of the Lord's house</hi> shall <hi type="italic">shortly</hi> be brought again, prophesied a lie (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">v. 16</reference>), yet he that said, They shall <hi type="italic">at length</hi> be brought again, prophesied the truth. We are apt to set our clock before God's dial, and then to quarrel because they do not agree; but the Lord is a God of judgment, and it is fit that we should wait for him.  <chapter eID="Jer.27"/> <div eID="gen17811" type="x-p"/>

entries.ac28f4659bedf97c428d41b3b26f132f32c3573a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10171"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.27.1-Jer.27.22">Jr 27:1-22</reference>. The Futility of Resisting Nebuchadnezzar Illustrated to the Ambassadors of the Kings, Desiring to Have the King of Judah Confederate with Them, under the Type of Yokes. Jeremiah Exhorts Them and Zedekiah to Yield.</title> <div sID="gen18147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10171"/><hi type="bold">1. Jehoiakim--</hi>The prophecy that follows was according to this reading given in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, fifteen years before it was published in the reign of Zedekiah to whom it refers; it was thus long deposited in the prophet's bosom, in order that by it he might be supported under trials in his prophetic career in the interim [Calvin]. But "Zedekiah" may be the true reading. So the Syriac and Arabic Versions. <reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">Jr 27:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jr 28:1</reference>, confirm this; also, one of Kennicott's manuscripts. The English Version reading may have originated from <reference osisRef="Jer.26.1">Jr 26:1</reference>. "Son of Josiah" applies to Zedekiah as truly as to "Jehoiakim" or "Eliakim." The fourth year may, in a general sense here, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jr 28:1</reference>, be called "the beginning of his reign," as it lasted eleven years (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18">2Ki 24:18</reference>). It was not long after the fourth year of his reign that he rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jr 51:59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.3">52:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.20">2Ki 24:20</reference>), in violation of an oath before God (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>). <div eID="gen18147" type="x-p"/>
entries.687e5b38ec711184f8113977c666b30281287902: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10172"/><div sID="gen18148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10172"/><hi type="bold">2. bonds--</hi>by which the yoke is made fast to the neck (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.5">Jr 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen18148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yokes--</hi>literally, the carved piece of wood attached at both ends to the two yokes on the necks of a pair of oxen, so as to connect them. Here the yoke itself. The plural is used, as he was to wear one himself, and give the others to the ambassadors; (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">Jr 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.10">28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.12">12</reference>) proves that the symbolical act was in this instance (though not in others, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jr 25:15</reference>) actually done (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.20.2">Is 20:2</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.3">Eze 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.18">11, 18</reference>). <div eID="gen18149" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ae61d33bfc95e164c7b34c6cbb6ab10d0229e71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10173"/><div sID="gen18150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10173"/><hi type="bold">3. And send them to the king of Edom, &c.--</hi>Appropriate symbol, as these ambassadors had come to Jerusalem to consult as to shaking off the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar. According to Pherecydes in Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 567], Idanthura, king of the Scythians, intimated to Darius, who had crossed the Danube, that he would lead an army against him, by sending him, instead of a letter, a mouse, a frog, a bird, an arrow, and a plough. The task assigned to Jeremiah required great faith, as it was sure to provoke alike his own countrymen and the foreign ambassadors and their kings, by a seeming insult, at the very time that all were full of confident hopes grounded on the confederacy. <div eID="gen18150" type="x-p"/>
entries.04e21ff26d553d54b8b845f62466ef298b07ccb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10174"/><div sID="gen18151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10174"/>5. God here, as elsewhere, connects with the symbol doctrine, which is as it were its soul, without which it would be not only cold and frivolous, but even dead [Calvin]. God's mention of His supreme power is in order to refute the pride of those who rely on their own power (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.12">Is 45:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given it unto whom it seemed meet unto me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.115.15">Psa 115:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Da 4:17</reference>, 25, 32). Not for his merits, but of My own sole good pleasure [Estius]. <div eID="gen18152" type="x-p"/>
entries.2341d7f8c96bc2f06b6e621e2297b2f423e731d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10175"/><div sID="gen18153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10175"/><hi type="bold">6. beasts of the field--</hi>not merely the horses to carry his Chaldean soldiers, and oxen to draw his provisions [Grotius]; not merely the deserts, mountains, and woods, the haunts of wild beasts, implying his unlimited extent of empire [Estius]; but the beasts themselves by a mysterious instinct of nature. A reproof to men that they did not recognize God's will, which the very beasts acknowledged (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>). As the beasts are to submit to Christ, the Restorer of the dominion over nature, lost by the first Adam (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.1.28">Ge 1:28</reference>; 2:19, 20; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6-Ps.8.8">Psa 8:6-8</reference>), so they were appointed to submit to Nebuchadnezzar, the representative of the world power and prefigurer of Antichrist; this universal power was suffered to be held by him to show the unfitness of any to wield it "until He come whose right it is" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>). <div eID="gen18153" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9706ffbde1655ef74b43406cb784c75f5ae7633: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10176"/><div sID="gen18154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10176"/><hi type="bold">7. son ... son's son--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.20">2Ch 36:20</reference>). Nebuchadnezzar had four successors--Evil-merodach, his son; Neriglissar, husband of Nebuchadnezzar's daughter; his son, Labosodarchod; and Naboned (with whom his son, Belshazzar, was joint king), son of Evil-merodach. But Neriglissar and Labosodarchod were not in the direct male line; so that the prophecy held good to "his son and his son's son," and the intermediate two are omitted.<div eID="gen18154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time of his land--</hi>that is, of its subjugation or its being "visited" in wrath (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.22">Jr 27:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jr 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">50:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.26">Da 5:26</reference>).<div eID="gen18155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">serve themselves of him--</hi>make him their servant (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">Jr 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Is 13:22</reference>). So "his day" for the destined day of his calamity (<reference osisRef="Job.18.20">Job 18:20</reference>). <div eID="gen18156" type="x-p"/>
entries.44e70cf6e681bb9af280a4024e16c0ca3c1aaaed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10177"/><div sID="gen18157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10177"/><hi type="bold">8. until I have consumed them by his hand--</hi>until by these consuming visitations I have brought them under his power. <div eID="gen18157" type="x-p"/>
entries.b325c9cae9b56caa3241f9b0327a0bf80c21d863: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10178"/><div sID="gen18158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10178"/><hi type="bold">9. ye--</hi>the Jews especially, for whom the address to the rest was intended.<div eID="gen18158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enchanters--</hi>augurs [Calvin], from a root, the "eyes," that is, lookers at the stars and other means of taking omens of futurity; or another root, a "fixed time," observers of times: forbidden in the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Le 19:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">De 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">11, 14</reference>). <div eID="gen18159" type="x-p"/>
entries.8570c816b7c5ae601fa382c9cfedc3c689c4cde4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10179"/><div sID="gen18160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10179"/><hi type="bold">10. to remove you--</hi>expressing the event which would result. The very thing they profess by their enchantments to avert, they are by them bringing on you. Better to submit to Nebuchadnezzar, and remain in your land, than to rebel, and be removed from it. <div eID="gen18160" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ef8d18c15c5764d2cf162f4c45fc15415a00d46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10180"/><div sID="gen18161" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10180"/><hi type="bold">11. serve ... till it--</hi>The same Hebrew root expresses "serve" and "till," or "cultivate." Serve ye the king of Babylon, and the land will serve you [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18161" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd45d835322d4258997c23d3ebb6d724be6baa72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10181"/><div sID="gen18162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10181"/><hi type="bold">12. I spake also--</hi>translate, "And I spake," &c. Special application of the subject to Zedekiah. <div eID="gen18162" type="x-p"/>
entries.20fee7db5d4fb88b3e8061b9eac087bd0a91f6e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10182"/><div sID="gen18163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10182"/><hi type="bold">13. Why ... die--</hi>by running on your own ruin in resisting Nebuchadnezzar after this warning (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.31">Eze 18:31</reference>). <div eID="gen18163" type="x-p"/>
entries.30454ad8dbc8e4ffcf166b20521c31f956a4ab5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10183"/><div sID="gen18164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10183"/><hi type="bold">14. lie--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">Jr 14:14</reference>). <div eID="gen18164" type="x-p"/>
entries.98284055555c7faaae31036323a2cbd2a80f283f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10184"/><div sID="gen18165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10184"/><hi type="bold">15. in my name--</hi>The devil often makes God's name the plea for lies (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">Mt 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">7:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.15-Jer.27.20">Jr 27:15-20</reference>, the test whereby to know false prophets). <div eID="gen18165" type="x-p"/>
entries.9169cfd2e384d9fb7cd1644403106791f77c9dbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10185"/><div sID="gen18166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10185"/>16. The "vessels" had been carried away to Babylon in the reign of Jeconiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.13">2Ki 24:13</reference>); also previously in that of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.5-2Chr.36.7">2Ch 36:5-7</reference>). <div eID="gen18166" type="x-p"/>
entries.f50b086bb033c5b24f57ccd2c851969c61c35609: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10186"/><div sID="gen18167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10186"/><hi type="bold">18. at Jerusalem--</hi>that is, in other houses containing such vessels, besides the house of God and the king's palace. Nebuzara-dan, captain of the guard under Nebuchadnezzar, carried all away (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13-2Kgs.25.17">2Ki 25:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.18">2Ch 36:18</reference>). The more costly vessels had been previously removed in the reigns of Jehoiakim and Jeconiah. <div eID="gen18167" type="x-p"/>
entries.60001754f413fdace4decb9b18ca8ae6c4a09889: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10187"/><div sID="gen18168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10187"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jr 52:17</reference>, 20, 21). <div eID="gen18168" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1e7c37e02ec608f352163dc835d33713f07ddfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10188"/><div sID="gen18169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10188"/><hi type="bold">22. until ... I visit them--</hi>in wrath by Cyrus (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>). In seventy years from the first carrying away of captives in Jehoiachin's reign (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jr 29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.21">2Ch 36:21</reference>).<div eID="gen18169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">restore them--</hi>by the hand of Cyrus (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7">Ezr 1:7</reference>). By Artaxerxes (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.19">Ezr 7:19</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.27"/>

entries.8cbc58f7373c78a2a6adc77a9213eb17ff6aaf36: <div eID="gen30006" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30009" type="x-p"/> Ambassadors being come from several neighboring nations to solicit the king of Judah to join in a confederacy against the king of Babylon, Jeremiah is commanded to put bands and yokes upon his neck, (the emblems of subjection and slavery), and to send them afterwards by those ambassadors to their respective princes; intimating by this significant type that God had decreed their subjection to the Babylonian empire, and that it was their wisdom to submit. It is farther declared that all the conquered nations shall remain in subjection to the Chaldeans during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and those of his son and grandson, even till the arrival of that period in which the Babylonians shall have filled up the measure of their iniquities; and that then the mighty Chaldean monarchy itself, for a certain period the paramount power of the habitable globe, shall be voted with a dreadful storm of Divine wrath, through the violence of which it shall be dashed to pieces like a potter's vessel, the fragments falling into the hands of many nations and great kings, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.1-Jer.27.11">Jer 27:1-11</reference>. Zedekiah, particularly, is admonished not to join to the revolt against Nebuchadnezzar, and warned against trusting to the suggestions of false prophets, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.11-Jer.27.18">Jer 27:11-18</reference>. The chapter concludes with foretelling that what still remained of the sacred vessels of the temple should be carried to Babylon, and not restored till after the destruction of the Chaldean empire, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19-Jer.27.22">Jer 27:19-22</reference>. <div eID="gen30009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30010" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30011" type="x-p"/> In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim - It is most evident that his prophecy was delivered about the fourth year of Zedekiah, and not Jehoiakim, as in the text. See <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jer 28:1</reference>. Three of Kennicott's MSS. (one in the text, a second in the margin, and the third upon a rasure) have Zedekiah; so likewise have the Syriac and the Arabic. Houbigant, Lowth, Blayney, Dahler, and others declare for this reading against that in the present text. And it is clear from the third and twelfth verses, where Zedekiah is expressly mentioned, that this is the true reading.
entries.42ffe2cda6cf5bb0e549de59e7f24329ec5ba370: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30012" type="x-p"/> Make thee bonds and yokes - Probably yokes with straps, by which they were attached to the neck. This was a symbolical action, to show that the several kings mentioned below should be brought under the dominion of the Chaldeans.
entries.7b2c61d03ad56073208cee61e51aef3f9855667c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30013" type="x-p"/> I have made the earth - I am the Creator and Governor of all things, and I dispose of the several kingdoms of the world as seemeth best to me.
entries.30f28aef2a1ffa1bc8ecc731b5f554d9a33a63d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30014" type="x-p"/> And now have I given - These kingdoms are at my sovereign disposal; and at present, for the punishment of their rulers and people, I shall give them into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.
entries.42b70899b5c78490713e97da7a6bfa0ff9d34ee9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30015" type="x-p"/> And all nations shall serve him (Nebuchadnezzar), and his son, (Evil-merodach <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">Jer 52:31</reference>), and his son's son, (Belshazzar, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.11">Dan 5:11</reference>.) All which was literally fulfilled.
entries.3831b62eff4d429def8566f9c2066f53bb7514b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30016" type="x-p"/> Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets - Who pretend to have a revelation from heaven. <div eID="gen30016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30017" type="x-p"/> Nor to your diviners - קסמיכם kosemeychem, from קסם kasam, to presage or prognosticate. Persons who guessed at futurity by certain signs in the animate or inanimate creation. <div eID="gen30017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30018" type="x-p"/> Nor to your dreamers - חלמתיכם chalomotheychem, from חלם chalam, to break in pieces; hence חלום chalom, a dream, because it consists of broken fragments. Dream-interpreters, who, from these broken shreds patch up a meaning by their own interpolations. <div eID="gen30018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30019" type="x-p"/> Nor to your enchanters - ענניכם oneneychem, from ענן anan, a cloud - cloud-mongers. Diviners by the flight, color, density, rarity, and shape of clouds. <div eID="gen30019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30020" type="x-p"/> Nor to your sorcerers - כשפיכם cashshapheychem, from כשף kashaph, to discover; the discoverers, the finders out of hidden things, stolen goods, etc. Persons also who use incantations, and either by spells or drugs pretend to find out mysteries, or produce supernatural effects. Every nation in the world had persons who pretended to find out hidden things, or foretell future events; and such were gladly encouraged by the ignorant multitude; and many of them were mere apes of the prophets of God. Man knows that he is short-sighted, feels pain at the uncertainty of futurity, and wishes to have his doubts resolved by such persons as the above, to put an end to his uncertainty.
entries.872e852164025b85fd21e16809b9a426b6ef75cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30021" type="x-p"/> Why will ye die - If ye resist the king of Babylon, to whom I have given a commission against you, ye shall be destroyed by the sword and by famine; but if ye submit, ye shall escape all these evils.
entries.03690dfb35b6eef3a1fdc2111d02f890c2070d62: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30022" type="x-p"/> The vessels of the Lord's house - Which had been carried away by Nebuchadnezzar under the reigns of Jehoiakim and Jeconiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.7-2Chr.36.10">2Chr 36:7-10</reference>. <div eID="gen30022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30023" type="x-p"/> Shall now shortly be brought again - This is a lie. They shall not be restored till I bring them up, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.22">Jer 27:22</reference>, which was after the captivity, when they were sent back by Cyrus, the Lord inclining his heart to do it, <reference osisRef="Ezr.1.7">Ezr 1:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezr.7.19">Ezr 7:19</reference>.
entries.39683987098ff4968026f5632a55d1d44594ab42: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30024" type="x-p"/> Concerning the pillars - Two brazen columns placed by Solomon in the pronaos or portico of the temple, eighteen cubits high, and twelve in circumference, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.16-1Kgs.7.22">1Kgs 7:16-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>. <div eID="gen30024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30025" type="x-p"/> The sea - The brazen sea, ten cubits in diameter, and thirty in circumference. It contained water for different washings in the Divine worship, and was supported on twelve brazen oxen. Perhaps these are what are called the bases here. See the parallel places at <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13">2Kgs 25:13</reference> (note), etc.; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jer 52:17</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Jer.52.20-Jer.52.21">Jer 52:20-21</reference> (note), and the notes on them.
entries.17e9bd848c778d5bf8ff1e61ed704ca90885a535: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30026" type="x-p"/> They shall be carried to Babylon - Far from those already taken being brought back, those which now remain shall be carried thither, unless ye submit to the Chaldeans. They did not submit, and the prophecy was literally fulfilled; see <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:17-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.13">2Kgs 25:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.18">2Chr 36:18</reference>.  <chapter eID="Jer.27"/> <div eID="gen30026" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce8c429612869d3a51932996b9fc6ff80ea77199: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.1">Jer 27:1</reference> <div eID="gen14156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14157" type="x-p"/> The Yoke of Babylon. - In three sections, connected as to their date and their matter, Jeremiah prophesies to the nations adjoining Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.2-Jer.27.11">Jer 27:2-11</reference>), to King Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.12-Jer.27.15">Jer 27:12-15</reference>), and to the priests and all the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.16-Jer.27.22">Jer 27:16-22</reference>), that God has laid on them the yoke of the king of Babylon, and that they ought to humble themselves under His almighty hand. <div eID="gen14157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14158" type="x-p"/> According to the (corrected) heading, the prophecy was given in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah. If we compare Jer 28 we find the same date: "in that year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah," more fully defined as the fourth year of his reign. Graf has made objection, that in the case of a reign of eleven years, one could not well speak of the fourth year as the beginning of the reign. But the idea of beginning is relative (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>), and does not necessarily coincide with that of the first year. The reign of Zedekiah is divided into two halves: the first period, or beginning, when he was elevated by Nebuchadnezzar, and remained subject to him, and the after or last period, when he had rebelled against his liege lord.
entries.f0d78323a7ba699548216a97446ccf61a5c9e308: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.2-Jer.27.8">Jer 27:2-8</reference> <hi type="italic">The yoke of the king of Babylon upon the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. - </hi> Jer 27:2. <hi type="italic">"Thus said Jahveh to me: Make thee bonds and yokes, and put them upon thy neck, </hi> Jer 27:3. <hi type="italic">And send them to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon, by the hand of the messengers that are come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah. </hi> Jer 27:4. <hi type="italic">And command them to say unto their masters, Thus hath Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel, said: Thus shall ye say unto your masters: </hi> Jer 27:5. <hi type="italic">I have made the earth, the man and the beast that are upon the ground, by my great power and by my outstretched hand, and give it to whom it seemeth meet unto me. </hi> Jer 27:6. <hi type="italic">And how have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant; and the beasts of the field also have I given him to serve him. </hi> Jer 27:7. <hi type="italic">And all nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his land come, and many nations and great kings serve themselves of him. </hi> Jer 27:8. <hi type="italic">And the people and the kingdom that will not serve him, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and that will not put its neck into the yoke of the king of Babylon, with sword, with famine, and with pestilence I will visit that people, until I have made an end of them by his hand. </hi> Jer 27:9. <hi type="italic">And ye, hearken not to your prophets, and your soothsayers, and to your dreams, to your enchanters and your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying: Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon. </hi> Jer 27:10. <hi type="italic">For they prophesy a lie unto you, that I should remove you far from your land, and that I should drive you out and ye should perish. </hi> Jer 27:11. <hi type="italic">But the people that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and will serve him, that will I let remain in its land, saith Jahveh, to till it and to dwell therein."</hi> <div eID="gen14158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14159" type="x-p"/> The yoke Jeremiah is to make and lay on his neck is a plain emblem of the Babylonian yoke the nations are to bear. The words "bonds and yokes" denote together one yoke. מטות are the two wooden beams or poles of the yoke, which were fastened together by means of the מוסרות, bonds, ropes, so that the yoke might be laid on the beast’s neck; cf. Lev 26:13. That Jeremiah really put such a yoke on his neck and wore it, we see from <reference osisRef="Jer.28.10">Jer 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.12">Jer 28:12</reference>, where a false prophet breaks it for him. He is to send the yoke to the kings of Edom, Moab, etc., by means of envoys of those kings, who were come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah. And since Jeremiah laid a yoke on his own neck, and so carried out the commanded symbolical action in objective reality, there is no reason to doubt that he made yokes for the five kings named and gave them to their respective envoys. Chr. B. Mich., Hitz., Graf, hold this to be improbable, and suppose that Jeremiah only made a yoke for himself and put it on his neck; but by appearing abroad with it, he set before the eyes of the ambassadors, the yoke that was to be laid on their kings, and, in a certain sense, emblematically gave it to them. But even though this might have sufficed to accomplish the aim of the prophecy, it is difficulty to reconcile it with the wording of the text; hence Hitz. seeks arbitrarily to change שׁלּחתּם into שׁלּחתּה. And it is a worthless argument that Jeremiah cannot possibly have believed that the envoys would carry the yokes with them and deliver them to their masters. Why should not he have believed they would do so? And if they did not, it was their concern. The plur. "bands and yokes" may indeed mean a single yoke, but it may also mean many; and the verbs נתתּם and שׁלּחתּם, both with plural suffixes, indicate clearly that he was to make not merely one yoke for himself, but yokes for himself and the kings. In <reference osisRef="Jer.28.10">Jer 28:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.28.12">Jer 28:12</reference>, where <hi type="italic">one</hi> yoke is spoken of, the singular המּוטה is used; while, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.13">Jer 28:13</reference>, "yokes of wood hast thou broken," does not prove that this plural has the same force as the singular. <div eID="gen14159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14160" type="x-p"/> We are not told for what purpose ambassadors from the kings named had come to Jerusalem; but we can discover what it was from the message Jeremiah gives them for their lords. From this it appears, without a doubt, that they were come to take counsel as to a coalition with the view of throwing off the Chaldean supremacy. By God’s command Jeremiah opposes this design with the announcement, that the God of Israel, the Creator of the world and of all creatures, has given all these lands (those of the kings named in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">Jer 27:3</reference>) into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar; that men, and even beasts, should serve him, i.e., that he might exercise unbounded dominion over these lands and all that belonged to them, cf. Jer 28:14. "My servant," as in Jer 25:9. All nations are to serve him, his son and his grandson. These words simply express the long duration of the king of Babylon’s power over them, without warranting us in concluding that he was succeeded on the throne by his son and his grandson, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.6.2">Deu 6:2</reference>; Deu 4:25. For, as we know, Nebuchadnezzar was succeeded by his son Evil-Merodach; then came his brother-in-law Neriglissar, who murdered Evil-Merodach, who was followed by his son Laborosoarchod, a child, murdered after a nine months’ reign by conspirators. Of these latter, Neboned ascended the throne of Babylon; and it was under his reign that the time for his land came that it should be made subject by many nations and great kings, cf. Jer 25:14. גּם הוּא serves to strengthen the suffix on ארצו; and the suffix, like בּו, refers to Nebuchadnezzar.<note placement="foot"><reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jer 27:7</reference> is wanting in the lxx, and therefore Mov. and Hitz. pronounce it spurious. But, as Graf remarked, they have no sufficient reason for this, since, reference being had to <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">Jer 27:16</reference> and to <reference osisRef="Jer.28.3">Jer 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.11">Jer 28:11</reference>, this verse is very much in place here. It is not a <hi type="italic">vaticinium ex eventu</hi>, as Hitz. asserts, but was rather omitted by the lxx, simply because its contents, taken literally, were not in keeping with the historical facts. The lxx omit also the clause from "that will not serve" to "king of Babylon and," which is accordingly, and for other subjective reasons of taste, pronounced spurious by Hitz.; but Graf justly opposes this.</note> <div eID="gen14160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14161" type="x-p"/> What is said in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.6">Jer 27:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jer 27:7</reference> is made sterner by the threatening of <reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">Jer 27:8</reference>, that the Lord will punish with sword, famine, and pestilence the people and kingdom that will not serve Nebuchadnezzar. ואת introduces a second relative clause, the את being here quite in place, since "the people and the kingdom" are accusatives made to precede absolutely, and resumed again by the 'על הגּוי ה, which belongs directly to the verb "visit." With עד־תּמּי, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.24.10">Jer 24:10</reference> and אתם  עד־כּלּותי, corresponding in meaning, in Jer 9:15.
entries.f8d04c7dc6c71fd1566785a2ccb312ec5c0439fa: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.9-Jer.27.10">Jer 27:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen14161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14162" type="x-p"/> Therefore they must not hearken to their prophets, soothsayers, and sorcerers, that prophesy the contrary. The mention of dreams between the prophets and soothsayers on the one hand, and the enchanters and sorcerers on the other, strikes us as singular. It is, however, to be explained from the fact, that prophets and soothsayers often feigned dreams and dream-revelations (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.23.25">Jer 23:25</reference>); and other persons, too, might have dreams, and could give them out as significant. Cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.29.8">Jer 29:8</reference>, where dreams are expressly distinguished from the discourse of the prophets and soothsayers. Whether the reckoning of five kinds of heathen prophecy has anything to do with the naming of five kings (Hitz.), appears to us to be questionable; but it is certain that Jeremiah does not design to specify five different, i.e., distinct and separate, kinds of heathen divination. For there was in reality no such distinction. Heathen prophecy was closely allied with sorcery ad soothsaying; cf. Deu 18:9., and Oehler on the <hi type="italic">Relation of Old Testament Prophecy to Heathen Divination</hi> (Tüb. 1861). The enumeration of the multifarious means and methods for forecasting the future is designed to show the multitude of delusive schemes for supplying the lack of true and real divine inspiration. כּשּׁפים, equivalent to מכשּׁפים , the same which in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference> is used along with מעונן. The explanation of the last-mentioned word is disputed. Some take it from ענן, cloud = cloud-maker or storm-raiser; others from עין, eye = fascinator, the idea being that of bewitching with the evil eye; see on Lev 19:26. The use of the word along with מנחשׁ וּמכשּׁף, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>, favours the latter rendering, whereas no passage in which the word is used in the Old Testament supports the sig. storm-raiser. "That <hi type="italic">I</hi> should remove you," as is shown by the continuation of the infinitive by והדּחתּי. The false prophets delude the people, inducing them to rise in rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, contrary to God’s will, and thus simply bringing about their expulsion from their land, i.e., removal into banishment. למען shows, as frequently, that the inevitable consequence of these persons’ proceedings is designed by them.
entries.279013c913bef8cb1520b9daed6b6be4d76717da: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.11">Jer 27:11</reference> <div eID="gen14162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14163" type="x-p"/> The people, on the other hand, that bends under the yoke of the king of Babylon shall remain in its own land. For the great Asiatic conquerors contented themselves, in the first place, with thoroughly subjecting the vanquished nations and imposing a tribute; only in the case of stubborn resistance or of insurrection on the part of the conquered did they proceed to destroy the kingdoms and deport their populations. This Zedekiah and the ambassadors that had come to him might have learnt from Nebuchadnezzar’s course of action after the capture of Jerusalem under Jehoiachin, as compared with that in Jehoiakim’s time, had they not been utterly infatuated by the lying spirit of the false prophets, whose prophecies accommodated themselves to the wishes of the natural heart.
entries.ce930a12c2c8e19ca6520ac30548dba5a0b552dd: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.12-Jer.27.15">Jer 27:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen14163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14164" type="x-p"/> To King Zedekiah Jeremiah addressed words of like import, saying: <hi type="italic">"Bring your necks into the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and ye shall live. </hi> Jer 27:13. <hi type="italic">Why will ye die, thou and thy people, by sword, famine, and pestilence, as Jahveh hath spoken concerning the people that will not serve the king of Babylon? </hi> Jer 27:14. <hi type="italic">And hearken not unto the words of the prophets that speak unto you: Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon; for they prophesy a lie unto you. </hi> Jer 27:15. <hi type="italic">For I have not sent them, saith Jahveh, and they prophesy in my name falsely, that I might drive you out and ye might perish, ye and the prophets that prophesy unto you."</hi> - The discourse addressed to the king in the plural, "bring your necks," etc., is explained by the fact that, as <reference osisRef="Jer.27.13">Jer 27:13</reference> shows, in and along with the king of his people are addressed. The imperative וחיוּ intimates the consequence of the preceding command. <reference osisRef="Jer.27.13">Jer 27:13</reference> gives the application of the threat in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.8">Jer 27:8</reference> to King Zedekiah and his people; and Jer 27:14. gives the warning corresponding to <reference osisRef="Jer.27.9">Jer 27:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.27.10">Jer 27:10</reference> against the sayings of the lying prophets; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">Jer 14:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">Jer 23:16</reference>, Jer 23:21.
entries.4a8336ce4495e9c516a6868b1c36c9966e331f01: <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16-Jer.27.22">Jer 27:16-22</reference> <div eID="gen14164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14165" type="x-p"/> The priests and all the people are warned to give no belief to the false prophesyings of a speedy restoration of the vessels carried off to Babylon. - Jer 27:16. <hi type="italic">"Thus hath Jahveh said: Hearken not to the sayings of your prophets that prophesy unto you: Behold, the vessels of Jahveh’s house shall now shortly be brought again from Babylon; for they prophesy a lie unto you. </hi> Jer 27:17. <hi type="italic">Hearken not unto them; serve the king of Babylon and live; wherefore should this city become a desert? </hi> Jer 27:18. <hi type="italic">But if they be prophets, and if the word of Jahveh be with them, let them now make intercession to Jahveh of hosts, that the vessels which are left in the house of Jahveh, and in the king’s house, and in Jerusalem, go not to Babylon. </hi> Jer 27:19. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jahveh of hosts concerning the pillars and the [brazen] sea and the frames, and concerning the other vessels that are left in this city, </hi> Jer 27:20. <hi type="italic">Which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took not away when he carried away captive Jechoniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah from Jerusalem to Babylon, with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem. </hi> Jer 27:21. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of Jahveh, and in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: </hi> Jer 27:22. <hi type="italic">To Babylon shall they be brought, and there shall they remain until the day that I visit them, saith Jahveh, and carry them up, and bring them back to this place."</hi> <div eID="gen14165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> Here Jeremiah gives King Zedekiah warning that the prophecies of a speedy end to Chaldean bondage are lies, and that confidence in such lies will hurry on the ruin of the state. He at the same time disabuses the priests of the hope raised by the false prophets, that the vessels of the temple and of the palace that had been carried off at the time Jechoniah was taken to Babylon will very soon be restored; and assures them that such statements can only procure the destruction of the city, since their tendency is to seduce king and people to rebellion, and rebellion against the king of Babylon means the destruction of Jerusalem - a prophecy that was but too soon fulfilled. The vessels of the temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.16">Jer 27:16</reference>, are the golden vessels Solomon caused to be made (1Ki 7:48.), which Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon, 2Ki 24:13. מבּבלה, from towards Babylon, i.e., from Babylon, whither they had been taken; cf. Ew. §216, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. "Now shortly," lit., hastily or speedily, i.e., ere long, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.28.3">Jer 28:3</reference>, where the prophet Hananiah foretells the restoration of them within two years, in opposition to Jeremiah’s affirmation that the exile will last seventy years.<note placement="foot">These words are not given in lxx, and so Mov. and Hitz. pronounce them spurious. Haev., on the other hand, and with greater justice, says (<hi type="italic">Introd</hi>. ii. 2), that the lxx omitted the words, because, according to an Alexandrian legend, the temple furniture was really very soon restored, even in Zedekiah’s time, cf. Baruch 1:8ff.; so that the false prophets were in the right. The passage cited from Baruch does not indeed give a very rigorous proof of this. It alleges that the silver vessels which Zedekiah had caused to be made after Jechoniah’s exile had been brought back by Baruch. But considering the innumerable arbitrary interferences of the lxx with the text of Jeremiah, the omission of the words in question cannot justify the slightest critical suspicion of their genuineness.</note> <div eID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14167" type="x-p"/> To show more clearly the irreconcilableness of his own position with that of the false prophets, Jeremiah further tells what true prophets, who have the word of Jahveh, would do. They would betake themselves in intercession to the Lord, seeking to avert yet further calamity or punishment, as all the prophets sent by God, including Jeremiah himself, did, cf. Jer 7:16. They should endeavour by intercession to prevent the vessels that are still left in Jerusalem from being taken away. The extraordinary expression לבלתּי באוּ has probably come from the omission of Jod from the verb, which should be read יבאוּ. As it stands, it can only be imperative, which is certainly not suitable. לבלתּי is usually construed with the infinitive, but occasionally also with the <hi type="italic">temp. fin</hi>.; with the imperf., which is what the sense here demands, in <reference osisRef="Exod.20.20">Exo 20:20</reference>; with the perf., Jer 23:14. - Of the temple furniture still remaining, he mentions in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">Jer 27:19</reference> as most valuable the two golden pillars, <hi type="italic">Jachin</hi> and <hi type="italic">Boaz</hi>, 1Ki 7:15., the brazen sea, 1Ki 7:23., and המּכונות, the artistic waggon frames for the basins in which to wash the sacrificial flesh, 1Ki 7:27.; and he declares they too shall be carried to Babylon, as happened at the destruction of Jerusalem, 2Ki 25:13. (בּגלותו for בּהגלותו.)<note placement="foot">The statement in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19-Jer.27.22">Jer 27:19-22</reference> is wide and diffuse; it is therefore condensed in the lxx, but at the same time mutilated. From the fact Mov., with Hitz. agreeing thereto, concludes that the Hebr. text has been expanded by means of glosses. Graf has already shown in reply to this, that the hand of a later glossator interpolating materials from <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jer 52:17</reference>; 2Ki 24:13 and 2Ki 24:1 is not betrayed in the extended account of the furniture remaining, and of the occasion on which it was left behind. He goes on to show that it is rather the editorial hand of Baruch than the hand of the glossator that is to be presumed from the fact that, in consequence of the narrative part of <reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">Jer 27:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">Jer 27:19</reference> is repeated in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.21">Jer 27:21</reference>; and from the further fact that it is impossible here to discriminate the interpolated from the original matter. Graf has also so conclusively proved the worthlessness of the distinguishing marks of the glossator adduced by Mov. and Hitz., that we adopt in full his argument. Such marks are (we are told), (1) the <hi type="italic">scriptio plena</hi> of מכונות here, as contrasted with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jer 52:17</reference>; 2Ki 25:13; <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.14">2Ch 4:14</reference>, and of יכוניה, as against <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.1">2Ch 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.4">2Ch 28:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.2">2Ch 29:2</reference>; and yet the interpolations in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">Jer 27:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.27.20">Jer 27:20</reference> are said to have been taken directly from <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jer 52:17</reference> and Jer 24:1. (2) The expression חרים, which is alleged not to have come into use till the exile. But the fact of its standing here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jer 39:6</reference> is enough to show it to have been earlier in use; cf. also 1Ki 21:8, 1Ki 21:11; and since it is <hi type="italic">not</hi> used in <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1">Jer 24:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.29.2">Jer 29:2</reference>, it is certain that it has not been got from there. (3) The "slip-shod" וירושׁלים, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.21">Jer 27:21</reference>, for ובירושׁלים, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">Jer 27:18</reference>, which is, however, occasioned simply by the preceding accusative of place, 'בית יהוה וגו (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">Jer 27:18</reference> also בּבית יהוה).</note>  <chapter eID="Jer.27"/> <div eID="gen14167" type="x-p"/>

entries.a849aafe168a195ed994a7f668f04dd83d193096: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.27.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.27.1" sID="gen59712" type="section"/> <div sID="gen59713" type="x-p"/>Jeremiah prefaces this prediction by saying, that it was delivered to him at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign. But this beginning, as we have said, extended to the whole of his reign while it was prosperous and entire. While, then, Jehoiakim enjoyed a quiet possession of the kingdom, Jeremiah was bidden to make known what had been committed to him, not to Jehoiakim himself, but, as we learn from the third verse, to Zedekiah who had not immediately succeeded him, but became at last king after various changes. God, then, committed this prophecy to his servant, but did not design it to be immediately promulgated. If it be asked, why God designed what he purposed to be made known to be concealed for so long a time? the answer is this, — that it was done for the sake of the Prophet himself, in order that he might with more alacrity perform his office, knowing of a certainty that no one thought that it could ever happen, and certainly the thing was incredible. <note n="177"> <div sID="gen59714" type="x-p"/> The manner in which Calvin accounts for this prophecy being so long kept hid is ingenious; but modern authors are not satisfied. Lightfoot says, that Jeremiah was ordered to make these yokes in Jehoiakim’s time to signify the subjection of Judah to the king of Babylon, but that he was ordered to send them to foreign kings in the reign of Zedekiah. The first verse is omitted in the Sept.; the Greek version as given by Theodoret, has “Jehoiakim,” and so the Vulg. and the Targ., but the Syr. and Arab. have “Zedekiah;” and there are three Hebrew MSS. in which the same is found. What seems most decisive is the beginning of the next chapter, where Hananiah comes forward in “the fourth year” of Zedekiah and breaks the yoke of Jeremiah. Gataker, Henry, Lowth, Scott, and Blayney, are all inclined to think that the mistake originally was that of the scribe. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen59714" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen59713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59715" type="x-p"/>God’s design then was to communicate this to his Prophet himself, that he might see afar off what no one, as I have just said, had thought could ever come to pass. This is the reason, as I think, why this prophecy was not immediately published, but was like a treasure deposited in the Prophet’s bosom, until the ripened time came. I shall defer till tomorrow the explanation of this prophecy.<div eID="gen59715" type="x-p"/><div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.27.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen59712" osisID="Jer.27.1" type="section"/><div eID="gen59699"/> <div sID="gen59716"/> <div sID="gen59717" type="x-p"/>PRAYER<div eID="gen59717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59718" type="x-p"/>Grant, Almighty God, that when at any time thou grievously threatenest us, we may not, on that account, become angry, but learn to acknowledge our sins, and truly to humble ourselves under thy mighty hand, and also to deprecate thy wrath, and to prove by true repentance, that we profit by thy word, and believe thy denunciations, so that we may become partakers of that mercy, through which thou promisest to be propitious to all who turn to thee: and may we thus advance more and more, and persevere in the right course of repentance, until having at length put off all the vices of the flesh, we shall attain to a perfection of righteousness and the fruition of that glory which has been laid up for us in heaven by Jesus Christ our Lord. — Amen.<div eID="gen59718" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen59716"/> <div sID="gen59719"/> <div sID="gen59720" type="x-p"/>Lecture one Hundred and Third<div eID="gen59720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen59721" type="x-p"/>We explained yesterday why this command was given to Jeremiah at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, which was not yet to be executed until the time of Zedekiah: it was God’s design to strengthen him in the meantime, lest he should faint in his course. Let us now see what was the object of this prophecy and what is its meaning.<div eID="gen59721" type="x-p"/>
entries.15162cfa2e706c47e9bdceb52fd7fa2cc3b13a99: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.27.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.27.3" sID="gen59722" type="section"/> <div sID="gen59723" type="x-p"/>The Prophet seems to have addressed the ambassadors who were sent by neighboring kings to King Zedekiah; and he was bidden to command them to declare each to his master, that they were all to come under the yoke of the king of Babylon. There is, moreover, no doubt but that God designed especially and chiefly to give a lesson to Zedekiah and to the Jews; for these legations mentioned here might have so emboldened them as to despise all prophecies, and to think themselves beyond all danger.
